pages.text:
How a case file works
Every case in this book is a real event from Australian history. Something happened. People
who were there told different stories. Some people were never asked at all. Your job is to read
the file, ask careful questions, and write a finding. There is no answer at the back. Eureka
Stockade, 1854 — Who fired first? — is the worked example (Case 5). Every other case is built
the same way.

Part                            What you do
1. The opener                   A short story, written to look authentic. In the Eureka case this is Nell’s
                                Diary, a child’s notebook that stops at the first shot. What’s true — who
                                is made up, who is real, and what isn’t certain — sits only in the teacher
                                notes, not on the story pages themselves.


2. Read                         Read the opener through to the moment in dispute.


3. Ask                          A short account of what is agreed, then three real witnesses on one page.
                                Each has a period portrait, or a plain silhouette if none exists, a short
                                summary of what they said, the source, and the same three questions:
                                What did they say they saw? Could they really have seen it? Why might
                                they say it?


4. Decide                       Write one finding in a My finding box. In the Eureka case: Who fired
                                first? Rebels, soldiers, or we can’t know — and why.


5. Super Sleuths                For students who want to dig deeper: the full witness files under seven
(optional)                      headings, a source pack, a timeline, evidence for and against, what we
                                still can’t know, and a sure / maybe / guess check. This page is reached
                                by a hyperlink, not a QR code.


 RULES FOR EVERY CASE
 Real sources only. Words in quotation marks come from a named record. Do not invent what the
 sources do not say.
 Never invent likenesses. Do not generate or invent a likeness of a real person. Use a real period
 portrait that is free to reuse, or a plain silhouette with a name card.
 Flag conflicts. Where the records disagree, say that they disagree. Leave open what the record
 leaves open. Do not resolve a dispute the sources do not settle.
 Teacher notes. What’s true — who is made up, who is real, what isn’t certain, the care the case
 needs, and the source and rights of each picture — sits only in the teacher notes, not on the opener’s
 student pages.

Our tent, Eureka
Sunday, 3 December. Before dawn.
Something woke me. A sound? Da was snoring. Ma
was asleep with the baby. Outside, the sky was
turning from black to the dark grey just before
dawn.
Then I heard it again. Feet. Lots of feet. Moving
together. And the soft jingle of harness, as if
horses were being walked very slowly.
I crept to the tent flap and lifted the corner.
Out in the grey half-light, beyond the stockade, a
long line of shapes was spreading out. They were
moving forward. Quietly. Steadily. Closer.
I opened my mouth to call Da. Someone somewhere
shouted a warning.
CRACK! A shot split the dark.
Was it from the stockade? From the soldiers? From
somewhere off in the bush? In the grey light, with

CASE 5 · YEAR 5 · THE CASE
Who fired first?
Eureka Stockade, Ballarat, 3 December 1854
Before dawn on Sunday 3 December 1854, soldiers and police marched from the Government Camp at
Ballarat to a stockade built by gold diggers on the Eureka lead. Captain Thomas led 276 men. Inside the
stockade there were far fewer diggers. Shooting broke out. Within minutes it was over. Everyone agrees
there was shooting. Not everyone agrees who started it.
Nell’s Diary stops at the first shot. These three people were there. Each left a real record. Ask each one:
What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? · Why might they say it?

                            Peter Lalor
                            The diggers’ leader. Inside the stockade.
                            Lalor was inside the stockade when the shooting began. About four months later he wrote
                            to the newspapers: “I believe that one or two signal shots were fired by our sentries.” He
                            also wrote: “The military fired the first volley.” A signal shot is a warning. A volley is many
                            guns fired together. Notice the words “I believe”: he is not sure about the sentry shots.
                            Source: Peter Lalor, “To the Colonists of Victoria”, Geelong Advertiser, 9 April 1855, and The Argus, 10 April
                            1855, p. 7.
    Peter Lalor, 1856       What did they say they saw? ______________________________
                            Could they really have seen it? ______________________________

                            Captain John Wellesley Thomas
                            Commander of the soldiers and police.

Teacher Note
Curriculum link: Australian Curriculum: HASS v9, Year 5
(History)
AC9HS5K03: “the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations
Australians and those who migrated to Australia, in the development of events in an
Australian colony”. A listed elaboration names “the impact of the Eureka Stockade on the
development of democracy”, and another poses “What if Peter Lalor had encouraged gold
miners to pay rather than resist licence fees?”

Skills: AC9HS5S02, “to locate, collect and organise information and data from primary
and secondary sources in a range of formats”; AC9HS5S04, “to evaluate primary and
secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives”. Also supports
AC9HS5S01 (developing questions) and the civics description AC9HS5K07 (citizens
working together towards a civic goal).


What’s true? Nell’s Diary
This note is for teachers. It is not printed in the student-facing diary, which is written to
look authentic.

Who is made up? Nell, her father, mother and the baby are invented, as are the trooper
at the licence hunt, Nell borrowing an onion, everything the Byrnes say and do, her class-
work headings, the place lines at the head of each entry, and Mrs Hayes’s margin notes,
hint notes, spelling corrections and words to Nell. The Byrnes are Irish, like many families
near the Eureka lead. Chinese diggers worked the Ballarat goldfield and paid licence fees,
but no particular Chinese person here is named or invented.

Who is real? Peter Lalor, Captain John Wellesley Thomas, Raffaello Carboni, Anastasia
Hayes and Timothy Hayes were all real. Their actions come from the case-file sources.
Lalor’s words on the stump are retold, not quoted; the oath, kneeling and “Amen” come
from Carboni’s 1855 book. Later notices say she pushed through the soldiers to reach her
chained husband and told his guards what she thought of them, but her exact words are not
certain. A later tradition credits Anastasia Hayes with helping to sew the Southern Cross
flag. That claim is disputed. She is also said to have nursed the wounded.

The school and the sketch Mrs Hayes taught at the Roman Catholic school Dean
Matthew Downing opened on 1 April 1853 in the slab-and-canvas St Alipius chapel, Ballarat
East (now St Alipius Parish School, Victoria Street). The image on the diary is Eugene von
Guérard’s January 1854 sketch Catholic Chapel on the Gravel Pit Line, Ballarat, State
Library of Victoria, accession H12532 (this work is out of copyright; no copyright
restrictions apply): https://viewer.slv.vic.gov.au/?entity=IE1446748 The spelling is Alipius.

Sources: https://saballarat.catholic.edu.au/st-alipius-history.html and
https://eurekapedia.org/Anastasia_Hayes.

What really happened? From the records: the licence hunts; licences burnt on Bakery
Hill on 29 November; stone-throwing on 30 November; the oath under the flag; the slab
stockade; the notice about lights; Carboni frying steak and noting the empty stockade on
Saturday; and the soldiers’ silent march before dawn on 3 December. From her tent, Nell
could not have known the soldiers’ numbers or their time of march. She only saw what she
could see, in the dark.

What isn’t certain? Witnesses disagree on the time of the attack. Nobody knows exactly
how many died: diggers, soldiers, and at least one woman. People still argue about who
sewed the flag (women of the goldfields, or tent makers or men using tent cloth) and who
fired first.

What happened next? The stockade was taken in minutes. Lalor was badly wounded
and hidden by friends. Thirteen men, including Timothy Hayes and Raffaello Carboni, were
tried for high treason in 1855 and found not guilty. The licence was soon replaced, and
Lalor was later elected to Victoria’s parliament.

Students may trust the diary as real. Reveal that Nell is invented and ask how they could
have checked.

An easy-read version in plain hand-print is available online (Easy-read switch) for
students who find the joined hand hard to read.


What’s true? The case
Peter Lalor, Captain John Wellesley Thomas and Raffaello Carboni were all real. The short
summaries use their own writing. Words in quotation marks come from Lalor’s 1855 letter,
Thomas’s report of 3 December 1854, and Carboni’s book of 1855. Nothing on the witness
page is a reconstruction.

Inquiry skills in this case
     Asking of every source: who wrote it, when, for whom, and were they there?
     Noticing careful words, such as “I believe”, “signal shot” and “volley”.
     Noticing Mrs Hayes’s questions in the margin of Nell’s Diary, and asking the
      same of the three witnesses.
     Recording disagreement without forcing an answer, and judging how sure a
      finding can be.

Running it in three lessons
    Lesson             What happens
    1. Read            Read Nell’s Diary together. Notice Mrs Hayes’s margin questions, such as
                       “How do you know?” and “What couldn’t you see?” The last entry breaks off
                       at the first shot. Teach: licence, stockade, sentry, volley.


    2. Ask             Read the short case page. Look at each witness’s picture, the short
                       summary, and the source. Answer the same three questions for Lalor,
                       Thomas and Carboni: What did they say they saw? Could they really have
                       seen it? Why might they say it?


    3. Decide          Students write a finding: Who fired first? Rebels, soldiers, or we can’t know
                       — and why. Share findings and compare. Close with: how did Eureka affect
                       the way the colony was governed?

pages.text:
Great Sandy Island, early July 1836

We have been on this sand for nearly three weeks now. The longboat is useless. Six of the men took what
they could carry and walked south. They said they would find Moreton Bay. We have heard nothing.

The people of this island came soon after we landed. They stood off at first, watching. When they saw
we had little food left they came closer. One older man pointed at the pandanus and made the sign for
eating. We gave him a brass button. He brought fish.

Eliza is still with us. Her husband the Captain is weaker every day. The wound in his shoulder has not
closed. She sits beside him most of the hours and does not speak much. When the women of the island
come she turns her face away. They have tried to cover her arms and shoulders with a mixture of grease
and charcoal. She will not let them. She says it is filthy. They shrug and leave her in the sun.

Yesterday two of the men who stayed with us were taken away with a party of the island people. They
went quietly. I do not know if they were asked or ordered. Eliza watched them go and said nothing.
Later she told me, very low, that she believes we are prisoners. I asked her how she knew. She said, “They
took our clothes. They make us carry wood. What else would you call it?”

I said the men who left us on the beach took more than the island people have. She did not answer.

This morning the Captain could not stand. Eliza held his head while he drank a little water the island
women had brought in a shell. One of them stayed and watched. Eliza did not thank her.

I am writing this on the back of a chart page. If anyone finds it, know that we are alive, that the island
people have not killed us, and that Eliza Fraser believes we are captives. I am no longer certain what I
believe.

The light is going. The women are calling the children in. Eliza has not moved from her husband’s
side.


                                                                                              C. Brown

CASE 23 · YEAR 9 · READ
Was Eliza Fraser a captive, or a guest?
The wreck of the Stirling Castle · K’gari, May–August 1836
Draft, pending consultation with the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation.
Read the letter through to the last line. Then read what the 1836 file can agree on. After that, three
people who were there will be asked the same three questions.


  CASE FILE: FRASER / STIRLING CASTLE
  Date of incident     May–August 1836
  Location          A coral reef north of Moreton Bay → K’gari (then Great Sandy Island)
  Status             Unresolved contradictions
  Key claims still disputed
  – Was Captain James Fraser speared, or did he die of starvation or injury?
  – Was Eliza Fraser a captive, or a guest who was kept alive?
  – Did the Butchulla people save the survivors, or mistreat them?
  – Which of Eliza’s later statements match the other survivors?


  WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1836 FILE, AND AFTER
  On the night of 21 May 1836 the brig Stirling Castle, James Fraser master, struck a coral reef well to
  the north of Moreton Bay. (Later writers often say Swain Reefs. That identification is disputed, and
  the wreck has not been found.) The survivors took to a longboat and a pinnace and headed south,
  hoping to reach the convict settlement at Moreton Bay. Some later accounts say Eliza, who was
  pregnant, gave birth in the leaking boat and that the baby lived only a short time. That claim is not in
  her official narrative of 6 September 1836, and it is not treated here as settled.
  The longboat was beached about twenty miles south of Sandy Cape, on the island Europeans called
  Great Sandy Island and the Butchulla people call K’gari, around mid-June. Some of the crew walked
  south toward Moreton Bay. Captain Fraser and the first mate, Charles Brown, both died after the
  landing. A rescue party from Moreton Bay, guided by the convict John Graham, brought Eliza Fraser,
  the second mate John Baxter, and other survivors out in mid-August. They had been on the island
  and the nearby mainland for roughly six to eight weeks.
  On 7 June 2023 the island’s official name was restored to K’gari.


Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber and other colours, used in Super Sleuths, mark what is
still disputed or was added later.

Three witnesses
The same three questions for each: What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? ·
Why might they say it? Each has a plain silhouette and a name card. No likeness of a real person has
been invented.

  A NOTE ON THE LANGUAGE OF THE RECORDS
  The 1836–37 records use the language of the period, including words that are offensive. They appear
  only as short, attributed quotations, not as the language of this case file.


A published Butchulla reading of these weeks is essential to the case, but it is not an 1836 eyewitness
statement. The 1836 file never asked the people who lived on K’gari, and this case will not invent a
speaker to fill the gap. Those perspectives belong in Super Sleuths, under “Not asked.”

                         Eliza Fraser
                         Eliza Anne Fraser · captain’s wife, survivor
                         A formal statement taken at Moreton Bay after the rescue.
                         Source. “Mrs Fraser’s Narrative. The Brig ‘Stirling Castle’,” Moreton Bay, 6 September 1836. Colonial
                         Secretary’s papers (NSW), item 33054-002544, State Library of Queensland / FromThePage. Out of
                         copyright.
                         What they said. “We were now portioned off to different masters, who employed us in
                              carrying, Wood, water and bark, and treated us with the greatest cruelty.” At the close of
A silhouette, not a likeness.
                              the same statement: “During the whole of my detention among the Natives I was treated
                              with the greatest cruelty…” When her husband lay dying, “I was always prevented from
                              approaching him or rendering him any assistance.” Graham, she wrote, “spoke to the
                              Natives for some time and after a good deal of altercation succeeded in getting me away.”
                         Could they really have seen it? She was there after the landing, and she was there when
                         Graham came. She was not on the pinnace after it parted. She could not see what Butchulla
                         people intended. The 1836 statement already speaks of detention and masters. The London book
                         of 1838 goes much further.
                         Why might they say it? In 1836 she was a newly widowed woman giving a formal statement at
                         a penal settlement, already the subject of a subscription. In 1837, in London, she stood to gain
                         public sympathy and money, and, the Australian Dictionary of Biography records, presented
                         herself as a penniless widow after she had remarried and had already been assisted in Sydney.

John Graham
                         John Graham · convict guide to the rescue party
                         A memorandum written to claim a reward, after the expedition.
                         Source. “Memorandum of the Real fact … of John Graham,” received 4 January 1837, Colonial Secretary’s
                         papers, item 33054-002543, SLQ / FromThePage. Supported by Fyans to the Colonial Secretary, 6
                         September 1836 (33054-002546), and by Lieutenant Otter’s letter, 27 August 1836 (33054-002547).
                         What they said. He writes that he “freed Mrs. Frazier from Seven hundred Canniballs
                              and savages” — the language of the penal colony, not a Butchulla account — but then
A silhouette, not a likeness.
                              describes how: “getting the tribes that claimed him as there friend to stand by him while he
                              claimed her as his or the (spirit of his wife) he succeeded to take her from than frightfull
                              place … and carried her upwards of 40 miles with the assistance of 4 blacks that came with
                              him from the mountains.” A note on the same memorandum explains “their belief of all
                              whites being spirits of their dead.” Fyans, who was not in the camp, added: “to him alone
                              are we indebted for the recovery of Mrs Frazer.”
                         Could they really have seen it? He had lived among Aboriginal people north of Moreton Bay
                         from 1827 to 1833 and, by his own and Otter’s account, could go into a camp unarmed. Otter
                         confirms that Graham came back “with four natives” and that Eliza was waiting close by for a
                         cloak. He was not a neutral observer.
                         Why might they say it? To obtain a remission or a reward, after “profferd Rewards and
                         Promises from Capt Fyans.” That interest is openly on the page. It does not cancel the detail
                         about a spirit-wife claim and Aboriginal assistance, which Otter independently places four
                         Aboriginal men at the handover.
                         What did they say they saw? ______________________________
                         Could they really have seen it? ______________________________
                         Why might they say it? ______________________________


                         Charles Otter
                         Lieutenant Charles Otter · 4th (King’s Own) Regiment
                         The official letter of the officer who led the rescue party.
                         Source. Letter to the Commandant, Moreton Bay, 27 August 1836, Colonial Secretary’s papers, item 33054-
                         002547, SLQ / FromThePage.
                         What they said. He first met two survivors on Bribie Island who, he says, “I at first took
                              to be natives as they were quite black and perfectly naked.” Of the later recovery: “Graham
                              appeared with four natives and gave us the satisfying intelligence that he had succeeded, &
A silhouette, not a likeness. that Mrs Fraser was waiting close at hand for a cloak to cover her, as she had been stripped
                              by the natives from the very first as well as the rest … many of whom had been very
                              unwilling to give her up.” Earlier in the same letter: “the natives who also brought the men
                         in had shown them more kindness then any other tribe.” Graham, he says, “was obliged not
                         only to go unarmed, but to strip himself perfectly naked when he went amongst them.”
                         Could they really have seen it? He saw the two men on Bribie, the handover on the sand,
                         and Eliza when she came to the party. He did not see the camp from which Graham brought her.
                         He waited at a prearranged mark in the sand. His phrase “in the hands of the natives” is his
                         official English. It sits in the same letter as “more kindness then any other tribe.”
                         Why might they say it? He was reporting to his commandant, recommending Graham, and
                         describing a “difficult and hazardous duty” the Governor later praised. He had reason to stress
                         danger and success. He also recorded kindness and Aboriginal assistance, which he did not have
                         to include.

Other people in the 1836 file, not on the Ask page, are named in Super Sleuths: John Baxter, Joseph Corralis, and
Robert Darge. Spellings in the file vary.

There is no answer at the back. You may say that “captive” and “guest” are both poor words for
what the sources describe. That is still a finding, not a refusal to think. The captivity narrative is
not to be retold as adventure. It is the thing under inquiry. Write only what these records can
support.

Was Eliza Fraser a captive, or a guest?
Circle one: A captive            ·   A guest       ·    We can’t know

  MY FINDING
  My reason:


  WHY IT STILL MATTERS
  Back in Sydney, then later in England, Eliza’s story was told and retold. Newspapers and
  pamphlets described “savages,” captivity, and horrors. Money was raised for her. Books
  appeared. The island came to be known as Fraser Island. Those sensational versions helped to
  shape colonial ideas about Aboriginal people along the coast. They also sold. In 2023 the island’s
  official name was restored to K’gari — a change the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation has
  described as respect, after a name taken away through disrespect. The wreck itself is
  straightforward. The weeks that followed, and what was later made of them, are not. That is why
  the file is still open.

Teacher Note
CASE 23 · YEAR 9 · ELIZA FRASER AND THE WRECK OF THE STIRLING CASTLE
 CONSULTATION REQUIRED
  This case is a draft, pending consultation with the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation, the RNTBC
  for K’gari, and with the families or Elders the Corporation names. It is not a finished student file.
  Follow the AIATSIS Code of Ethics and the AIATSIS guidelines for ethical publishing. No sacred
  or secret material. No invented Butchulla speaker, character, or likeness. Teacher preview
  required.


Curriculum link: Australian Curriculum: History v9, Year 9
AC9HH9K03: the causes and effects of European contact and extension of settlement,
including their impact on the First Nations Peoples of Australia. AC9HH9K06: different
experiences and perspectives of colonisers, settlers and First Nations Australians and the
impact of these experiences on changes to Australian society’s ideas, beliefs and values. Also
useful: skills AC9HH9S06 (compare perspectives in sources) and AC9HH9S07 (analyse
different and contested historical interpretations).


What’s true about the opener · the letter from Charles Brown
This note is for teachers. It is not printed on the letter’s student page, which is written to look
authentic. The page is not labelled invented, because the book’s standing rule is that what’s
true sits only here.

The letter is not a historical document. No letter from Charles Brown on Great Sandy Island is
known. He was real: the first mate (Eliza’s narrative; Baxter’s “Chief mate”; later scholarship).

Dramatic irony, not for the student page. Eliza’s official narrative says that after Captain
Fraser’s death she and Brown were put across to the mainland in a canoe; Brown, already terribly
injured (she describes burns with firebrands, and that “the flesh had fallen from his feet”), died
three or four days after the crossing. She says she was prevented from taking him food. The letter’s
line “know that we are alive, that the island people have not killed us” is written in a voice that does
not know that. Students should meet the letter first. Teachers may return to Brown’s death after the
witnesses, if they judge the class ready; it needs a content note.

Constructed scenes and details that were kept, because they carry the approved voice and are
not clearly contradicted, but are not in the 1836 statements: the brass button and the pandanus sign
(Eliza says fish were obtained in exchange for “articles of wearing apparel”); the grease and charcoal
on Eliza’s arms (a later interpretive reading of practical care, not a detail in the official file); the shell
of water; “two of the men who stayed with us were taken away” as a single witnessed scene; Brown’s
spoken uncertainty on the sand; the “back of a chart page.”

pages.text:
The shoulder wound. The letter says “The wound in his shoulder has not closed.” It does not say
he arrived on the island already wounded. Eliza attributes the wound to a spear, “a little below the
blade bone,” after they were already in a camp and he had been unable, through debility, to carry a
large log of wood. “Of this wound he never recovered,” and he died eight or nine days afterwards. In
an early-July letter, a wound that “has not closed” can fit a spearing earlier in the stay. Teachers
should not let students assume it was a wreck or boat injury.

Two wording changes only in the approved text. Everything else of the approved letter was kept.
1. The date line. “Late July 1836” became “early July 1836.” Eliza’s narrative of 6 September 1836
says they beached about twenty miles south of Sandy Cape “about three weeks since our departure
from the wreck” (the wreck was the night of 21 May, so around mid-June). Barbara Dawson, In the
Eye of the Beholder (ANU Press, 2014), gives about 12 June. The letter also says “We have been on
this sand for nearly three weeks now.” Early July keeps that sentence consistent with a mid-June
landing.
2. First contact. “The people of this island came on the third day” became “The people of this island
came soon after we landed.” Eliza’s official narrative: “Directly we landed the Natives came down in
crowds.” “They stood off at first, watching” was kept, as a constructed detail of cautious approach,
not as a delay of two days.
Other details flagged, not changed. “Six of the men… walked south.” Eliza does not give a
number. Dawson (2014) reconstructs six men walking south; three reached Moreton Bay. The
number six is a later reconstruction, not a figure in the 1836 statements. It was kept, with this flag,
because it is the scholarly number and is not clearly false.


What’s true? The case
Eliza Fraser, John Graham and Charles Otter were all real. The short summaries use their own
writing. Words in quotation marks come from Eliza’s narrative of 6 September 1836, Graham’s
memorandum received 4 January 1837, and Otter’s letter of 27 August 1836. The three images
are plain period-style silhouettes with name cards, not likenesses of the people named. No
period portrait from life has been invented for this file.

An optional Super Sleuths extension follows My finding, and is on the website at
robmac10.github.io/eliza-fraser-case/#sleuth. It reopens colour marking, reliability labels, the full
1836 witness files, published Butchulla perspectives under “Not asked,” and a more rigorous finding.
The Three Laws are cited from the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation’s “People & Country” page
(bac-kgari.org/people-and-country) and marked for consultation. They are not evidence of what any
named person said in 1836, and are not to be printed as a finished student extract until the
Corporation has been consulted.

Uncertainties · still open
The baby in the boat. In the ADB and some later histories; not in the 6 September 1836 official
narrative. Leave unsettled.

Bracewell and Russell. Still to be checked: locate the primary text of David Bracewell’s 1842
claim and Henry Stuart Russell’s version before citing them. Official 1836–37 records name
Graham, not Bracewell.

Where exactly the ship struck. A reef north of Moreton Bay, 21 May 1836, is agreed. Swain
Reefs is a common later identification, disputed by Geraghty (2021) in favour of Frederick Reef. The
wreck has not been found.

Dates of the recovery. Graham’s memorandum disagrees with itself. Otter’s letter is dated 27
August. The ADB gives the party’s return to Brisbane as 21 August 1836.

Names and spellings. Corralis / Corallas / Corrales / Carrallis; Youlden / Youldrow / Gouldron;
Dayman / Daymens; Darge / Dargo / Large. This draft uses one form on the student page and
records the variants here.

The 1837 London wording. A sentence often repeated, that the Lord Mayor had “never heard
anything so truly dreadful,” is cited by Iain McCalman from contemporary papers; verify against the
newspaper before quoting it in the finished case. It is not quoted here.

Butchulla wording in the finished case. Quote only page-exact, cleared extracts. The Three
Laws are cited from the Corporation’s website and marked for consultation.

Afterlives of the story. Modern Butchulla and scholarly readings (Foley, Behrendt, and others)
argue that the captivity-and-cannibal story fed a colonial picture of Aboriginal people and helped to
justify dispossession, including the name “Fraser Island.” That is an interpretation about afterlives,
not a finding the 1836 file can settle on its own.

Cultural safety · reminder
Consultation first, with the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation and those it names. Use K’gari for the

20 February 1965
                                                                                           Moree

Egg on my sleeve. I keep wiping it. Still there.

We came back. We had to. Last time they said the ban was off. We left. They put it
back on. I don’t know why I thought a meeting would be enough.

The crowd was already at the pool. Pressing in. So hot I could hardly breathe.
Someone spat. Then the tomatoes, the eggs. I have never been looked at like that.

I keep thinking we don’t live here. We’re from Sydney. We get on the bus. The
children don’t.

The police said if we stayed it would get worse. We stayed. I wanted to go. I hate
that I wanted to go.

Charlie wouldn’t move from the gate. They grabbed him. For a moment I couldn’t see
the kids and I thought —

I thought I would be braver than this.

One of the children was knocked down. They were frightened. So was I. What a thing
to come all this way and still be frightened.

They let them in, in the end. We went in too. For a minute it felt like winning. Then
we had to walk to the bus in a single line and they were still throwing things and
the windows kept getting hit.

A man at the bus said it quietly.

They’ll wait till you’re gone.

                                                                                    — on the bus

CASE 37 · YEAR 10 · READ
What happened in the towns the students visited,
and who recorded it?
The Freedom Ride · New South Wales, February 1965
Draft, pending consultation with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially Moree and
Walgett, and those they name, and with AIATSIS guidance.
Read the notebook page through to the last line. Then read what the 1965 file can agree on. After
that, three people will be asked the same three questions.

  CASE FILE: FREEDOM RIDE / 1965
  Date of incident      12–26 February 1965 (Moree visits: 16 and 19–20 February)
  Location          Regional New South Wales, including Walgett and Moree
  Status             Unresolved contradictions · Draft, pending consultation
  Key claims still disputed
  – What actually changed in the towns, and for how long?
  – Whose record should we trust — student diaries, local Aboriginal accounts, or the 1965
  newspapers and television?
  – When was the Moree baths ban really lifted?


  WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1965 FILE, AND AFTER
  Twenty-nine University of Sydney students left around midnight on 12 February 1965, as Student Action
  for Aborigines (SAFA). Charles Perkins, an Arrernte man, was president. Some left later and others joined.

  They travelled through regional New South Wales for about two weeks, using surveys, pickets and
  cameras, and they kept diaries. Newspapers, radio and television reported the trip as it happened.

  They went to Moree twice. On 16 February, Aboriginal children were at first refused the baths, then let in.
  That evening a public meeting voted 88 to 10 to remove the segregation clause.

  After they left, the old 1955 rule was enforced again. They returned on 19–20 February. A hostile crowd
  met them at the pool. Eggs, tomatoes and stones were thrown. Children and students went in, then left
  that night through the crowd.

  Local Aboriginal people were already campaigning in towns such as Walgett. The students met Harry Hall,
  president of the Walgett Aborigines’ Progressive Association, on 15 February.

  The Moree baths rule used the period language of racial exclusion. The wording is in Super Sleuths, with a
  content note. The ban was not settled in a single day.


Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.

CASE 37 · YEAR 10 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher note
Draft, pending consultation with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially
Moree and Walgett, and those they name, and with AIATSIS guidance.


The opener
The notebook is constructed. It is not an original 1965 page, and the handwriting is not original.
That fact belongs only in this teacher note, not on the student page. The writer is an unnamed city
student on the bus, in the spirit of diaries kept on the trip; the page is not Ann Curthoys’s diary and
must not be taught as hers. The date is 20 February 1965, the second Moree visit, after the first
meeting and after the ban was put back on. Scene details — the reimposed ban, the hostile crowd,
spit, eggs, tomatoes, stones, the police warning, Perkins taken from the gate, a child knocked down,
frightened children, going in, and leaving in single file while things were still being thrown — follow
Ann Curthoys’s contemporary diary (AIATSIS collection; published 2002) and Charles Perkins’s
later account of the return, as quoted on the AIATSIS Freedom Ride page. The draft’s “four nights
ago,” the 16 February date, the SAFA title, the method-explaining paragraph, the 88-to-10 vote, the
by-law wording, the number aboard, Gary Williams, and Lismore were taken off this page. They
belong in What is agreed, Super Sleuths, or this note.

Two short conversations in the source draft — a twelve-year-old who had never been inside, and a
woman from the mission — were invented details inside a known sequence. They have been cut.
Two scene lines were checked against the 20 February record and kept. “Charlie wouldn’t move
from the gate. They grabbed him.” Curthoys’s diary of the return, as quoted by AIATSIS, records:
“Charlie started talking to the crowd, but there was a lot of hissing and booing. Then he went to the
front of the line and when he refused to move was grabbed and taken away from the line.” Perkins,
in A Bastard Like Me (1975), also quoted by AIATSIS, places the struggle at the gate: “The mayor
ordered the police to have us removed from the gate entrance. They took hold of my arm and the
struggle started.” The notebook’s “from the gate” is a short compression of those two accounts of the
same confrontation. “One of the children was knocked down.” Curthoys’s diary, as quoted by
AIATSIS, records: “One child had been knocked down. The poor kids were very frightened.” She
wrote that the children told the students this, and that they had also been subjected to racist abuse
(the wording is not repeated on the student pages). Contemporary newspaper headlines of 21–22
February 1965 report a violent confrontation at Moree (among them the Daily Mirror, 21 February,
and the Sydney Morning Herald, 22 February). This file did not independently recover those two
exact phrases from a Trove article body. The closing is now: “A man at the bus said it quietly.” then
“They’ll wait till you’re gone.” Both the speaker and the line are constructed. The man is not a
named historical person. Do not teach either as a documented 1965 quotation. The line stands in for
a documented pattern: after the first Moree visit the ban was reimposed once the bus had left, and
later Moree memory records a similar fear. In 2025, Gomeroi man Uncle Darryl French, who was on
the bus to the pool on the return visit, recalled people saying that when the students left, local
people would have to deal with it (ABC News, 22 February 2025). Living people, including French,
are not given dates on the student pages.

pages.text:
Corrections and flags
Two Moree visits, not one. The source draft merged them. First visit, Wednesday 16 February
1965: a picket; children at first refused, then let in; an evening public meeting at the Memorial Hall,
initially hostile, at which a motion to remove the segregation clause was carried 88 votes to 10
(Curthoys’s diary, via AIATSIS; also ABC News, 2025). On 17 February, after the students had left,
Aboriginal children tried to get in after school; the mayor then said the 6 June 1955 statute would be
enforced (Curthoys, 18 February entry). In Tenterfield the students voted to return. Second visit,
Saturday 19–Sunday 20 February: a hostile crowd; eggs, tomatoes, stones, spit and scuffles; the
mayor said he would sign a motion to rescind, with conditions; children and students went in; they
left that night in single file (Curthoys’s diary; Perkins, A Bastard Like Me, via AIATSIS; ABC News,
2019 and 2025). Do not teach the ban as settled on 16 February. Curthoys later recalled that it took
about six months before the council formally rescinded the rule (ABC News, 27 September 2019).

Route and Lismore. The students left Sydney around midnight on Friday 12 February. A day-by-
day itinerary published by AIATSIS is: 12 Sydney; 13 Wellington; 14 Gulargambone; 15 Walgett; 16
Moree (first); 17 Boggabilla; 18 Tenterfield, then back; 19–20 Moree (return); 21 Grafton; 22
Lismore and Cabbage Tree Island; 23 Bowraville; 24 Kempsey; 25 Taree; 26 Sydney. They did not
leave for Lismore after the first Moree meeting. Some other lists add towns such as Warwick, Glen
Innes, Inverell or Coffs Harbour; treat those as a minor conflict in the route lists, not a problem to
resolve on the student page.

Numbers aboard. Twenty-nine students left Sydney on 12 February (University of Sydney;
Sydney Barani; AIATSIS). About 35 took part in all, because some left and others joined (AIATSIS).
Keep 29 as the departure figure, and flag that the complement changed.

By-law wording. The draft shortened the rule to “No person being a full-blooded or half-caste
aboriginal… shall use the baths.” ABC News (22 February 2025) quotes a fuller wording, used in
Super Sleuths with a content note. Wording and spelling vary slightly across later accounts; this file
has not checked the 1955 council instrument itself. The statute is often dated 6 June 1955
(Curthoys).

Gary Williams. A Gumbaynggirr-Bundjalung student, and one of two Aboriginal students at the
University of Sydney with Perkins. He was a member of SAFA, but he was not on the bus from
Sydney and he was not at either Moree visit. He was called home for a family emergency and joined
at Bowraville on 23 February, later confining his activism to locations on his own country
(University of Sydney, 2024; NSWALC; Sydney Barani; ABC News, 2025). The draft’s line that he
was “meant to join us later” and would “only come on the stretch that is his own country” over-
explains the delay. He is living: no dates on the student pages. He is named only in Super Sleuths
and this note.

Perkins’s words and graduation. “The problem is out in the open now” is kept, cited from
AIATSIS as said at the 1965 FCAATSI conference in Canberra, to about 200 people. This file has not
independently checked a 1965 conference transcript. The phrase “second class is not good enough”
appears in later interviews and education pages; it has not been pinned here to a 1965 primary
source, and it is not used on the student pages. Do not call Perkins “the first Aboriginal person to
graduate.” He graduated from the University of Sydney in 1966, and is often described as the first
Aboriginal man to do so; Margaret Valadian graduated from the University of Queensland in the

A misattributed quotation. The source draft gave Ann Curthoys the line that the ride “convinced

Wayne Nean and Aunty Sandra Buchanan, both living — are options for a future revision after
consultation, not extra cards in this draft.


Pictures, language, and care
The three images are plain mid-century-style silhouettes with name cards, not likenesses of the
people named. No portrait has been invented. A 1965 photograph of Perkins, from the State Library
of New South Wales Tribune set, appears on Wikimedia Commons as Flickr Commons “no known
copyright restrictions,” but the library catalogue also records courtesy of Tribune / SEARCH
Foundation. This draft uses a silhouette until rights and consultation are settled. Student pages
avoid slur-spelled-out language and keep violence at the level the diaries record (eggs, tomatoes,
stones, spit, shoving, a child knocked down). Teacher preview is required. Period wording appears
only as a short attributed extract, with a content note.


Consultation and teaching
Consultation first, with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited in 1965 — especially Moree
(Gamilaraay / Gomeroi) and Walgett (Wayilwan, Gamilaraay and Yuwaalaraay), and the other
communities on the route — and with those they name, following AIATSIS guidance. Use the
community’s own names for Country. Local protest did not begin when the bus arrived. Do not let a
Sydney student notebook stand in for a local Aboriginal account. AIATSIS Code of Ethics; guidelines
for ethical publishing; free, prior and informed consent; agreement on what may be quoted. No
sacred or secret material. This case is a draft, not a finished student file.

Friday, 28 June 1861.

                                                                             Cooper Creek


Clear, cold night; slight breeze from the E.; day beautifully warm

and pleasant. Mr Burke suffers greatly from the cold, and is

getting extremely weak. He and King start tomorrow up the creek …

it is the only chance we have of being saved from starvation.


I am weaker than ever, although I have a good appetite and relish

the nardoo much; but it seems to give us no nutriment …


Nothing now but the greatest good luck can save any of us; and as

for myself I may live four or five days if the weather continues

warm. My pulse is at forty-eight, and very weak, and my legs and

arms are nearly skin and bone. I can only look out, like Mr

Micawber, “for something to turn up.” Starvation on nardoo is by no

means very unpleasant, but for the weakness one feels, and the

utter inability to move oneself; for as far as appetite is concerned,

it gives me the greatest satisfaction.


                                                                                W. J. Wills

CASE 4 · YEAR 5 · READ
What was the real cause of death?
Burke and Wills at Cooper Creek, 1861
Draft, pending consultation with Yandruwandha Yawarrawarrka and related communities, and with
AIATSIS guidance.
Read the notebook page through to the last line. Then read what the 1861 file can agree on. After
that, three people will be asked the same three questions.

 CASE FILE: BURKE AND WILLS / 1861
 Date of incident April–September 1861 (depot: 21 April; last notebook: late June; King
 found: 15 September)
 Location          Cooper Creek, in Yandruwandha country
 Status            Unresolved contradictions · Draft, pending consultation
 Key claims still disputed
 – What was the real cause of death — hunger, the missed depot, the nardoo itself, the cold,
 or more than one of these?
 – Whose record should we trust — Wills’s notebook, King’s later narrative, or Howitt’s
 diary of the rescue?
 – What does the 1861 file leave unasked about the Yandruwandha people who kept King
 alive?


 WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1861 FILE, AND AFTER
 In 1860 a party left Melbourne to cross the continent from south to north. Robert O’Hara Burke led it.
 William John Wills was the surveyor. John King and Charles Gray went north with them from the Cooper
 Creek depot. (Some newspapers of the time wrote Grey. The expedition records usually write Gray.)

 The four reached the Gulf country and turned back. Gray died on 17 April 1861, on the return, before they
 reached the depot.

 On the evening of 21 April 1861, Burke, Wills and King reached the depot with two camels and almost no
 food. The depot party, led by William Brahe, had left that same morning. Stores had been buried, and a
 tree was marked so a returning party would know to dig. The exact wording cut into the tree is uncertain:
 sources disagree.

 They tried to make south towards Mount Hopeless, then came back to the creek. Both remaining camels
 died. They tried to live on nardoo — a fern seed used as food by the Yandruwandha people of the Cooper —
 and on fish and gifts they were given.

 On 30 May 1861 Wills went back to the depot and left a note in the buried cache. The depot was still
 empty. Unseen by him, Brahe and Wright had visited the cache earlier in May, thought it untouched, and
 left again. The wording of that 30 May note is in Super Sleuths. It is not the same document as the last
 notebook page at the front of this case.

 Wills’s last notebook entry is from late June 1861. He wrote that nardoo seemed to give them “no

pages.text:
nutriment,” that his pulse was at forty-eight, and that he could only look out, like Mr Micawber, “for
  something to turn up.” Burke and King then went up the creek for help, leaving food and water with him.

  Burke died a short time later. King later found Wills already dead. The exact days are not known. King was
  found alive on 15 September 1861 by Alfred Howitt’s relief party, after living with Yandruwandha people
  along the creek.

  In 1994, J. W. Earl and B. V. McCleary argued in the journal Nature that nardoo can destroy the vitamin
  thiamine, and that Burke and Wills may have died of beriberi as well as of hunger and cold. That is a later
  scientific reading, not something the 1861 file could know. It is still debated.


Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.

You have a notebook page, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The notebook is Wills’s own
last entry, shortened. It is not the whole record. Say what you think the real cause of death was,

What was the real cause of death?
Circle one: Hunger, after the depot party had gone · The nardoo itself (it seemed to give no
nutriment) · Hunger, cold, weakness, and the nardoo together · We can’t know which
mattered most


  MY FINDING
  My reason:


Why it still matters
Burke and Wills are still told as a heroic crossing, or as a bungled meeting at a tree. The file
is open because the records do not settle what killed them, and because the people who
kept King alive have not always been asked. Draft, pending consultation with

Super Sleuths
Optional, and a little harder. These questions stay in the file because the record is not settled.
You can also open them in the interactive book.
Open Super Sleuths in the app: robmac10.github.io/burke-wills-case/#sleuth


 THE LANGUAGE OF THE 1861 RECORDS
 Content note. The extracts below keep a few words from 1861 records that this case file does not use
 as its own, including “blacks” and “natives.” They are short, attributed quotations. They are not the
 language of this book.


 1 · TWO DIFFERENT DOCUMENTS
 Wills wrote the 30 May 1861 cache note at the depot and buried it in the camel-box cache (State
 Library of Victoria, MS 13071, SAFE 1, “Last notes”). A careful transcription of the two pages reads, in
 part:
 “Depot Camp, May 30th. We have been unable to leave the creek. Both camels are dead, and our
 provisions are exhausted. Mr Burke and King are down the lower part of the creek. I am about to
 return to them, when we shall probably come up this way. We are trying to live the best way we can,
 like the blacks, but find it hard work. Our clothes are going to pieces fast. Send provisions and clothes
 as soon as possible. W J Wills. The Depot party having left, contrary to instructions, has put us in this
 fix. I have deposited some of my journals here for fear of accidents. W J W.”
 That note does not contain “my pulse is at forty-eight,” “skin and bone,” or “it seems to give us no
 nutriment.” Those lines are from the later field notebook (NLA MS 30/7), used at the front of this
 case. Why does it matter if a later writer mixes the two documents into one page?


 2 · THE TREE, AND WHY NO ONE WAS WAITING
 King, in his 1861 narrative, remembered a tree marked “DIG, Apr 21.” Popular tellings often give
 “DIG 3 FT NW.” The Dig Tree site and later writers also record date blazes (including December 1860
 and 21 April 1861), a camp mark often read as B LXV (Burke, Camp 65), and a later mark by Howitt,
 AH DIG. A National Trust plaque notes that the Burke party recalled a depth of three feet, while
 some early settlers remembered forty feet. John White and later research list still more published
 variants. Brahe told the Commission he marked a tree with the date 21 April, and also a December
 date.
 Why was no one waiting at the Dig Tree? That was this case’s first outlined question. Brahe had
 already waited about four months. One of his party, Patton, was badly hurt. On 21 April he left for the
 Darling — the same morning the three men came in. In early May, Brahe and Wright returned,
 thought the cache untouched, and left again, before Wills came back on 30 May. What can we
 actually agree about the tree, and what is still in dispute?

pages.text:
3 · THE 1994 NATURE PAPER
J. W. Earl and B. V. McCleary, “Mystery of the poisoned expedition,” Nature 368 (21 April 1994):
683–684, argued that nardoo (Marsilea drummondii) contains thiaminase, an enzyme that destroys
vitamin B1 (thiamine), and that Burke and Wills may have died of beriberi as well as of hunger. An
earlier paper, McCleary and Chick, Phytochemistry 16 (1977), had identified thiaminase in nardoo.
Yandruwandha preparation of the seed is part of the argument: the explorers may not have prepared
it in the same way. John Hayman wrote a follow-up letter in Nature 370 (1994). The 1994 paper is a
hypothesis, not an autopsy, and it is still debated.
Wills himself had already written that the nardoo seemed to give “no nutriment,” and that he could
not understand it. How far can a later scientific paper settle a question the 1861 file left open?


4 · WHAT THE 1861 FILE DID NOT ASK
This draft does not put “the Yandruwandha people” on a witness card. A group is not one witness,
and this file is pending consultation with Yandruwandha Yawarrawarrka and related communities,
and with AIATSIS guidance.
Published starting points, for reading with community guidance, include: Benny Kerwin’s
Yandruwandha narrative, transcribed by Gavan Breen, in Luise Hercus and Peter Sutton (eds), This
Is What Happened: Historical Narratives by Aborigines (Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies,
1986); the listing for the Burke, Wills, King and Yandruwandha National Heritage Place (DCCEEW);
Wills’s diary for 3 June 1861, in which a man he names Pitchery feeds him fish and nardoo; and
King’s narrative of being fed, and of the people who wept over Burke’s remains and covered them
with bushes.
What is not asked if we only use the explorers’ notebooks? Whose skill kept King alive?


5 · BURKE’S LAST REQUEST, IN KING’S WORDS
In the narrative Howitt took down, King said that Burke, on the last evening, spoke these words: “I
hope you will remain with me here till I am quite dead — it is a comfort to know that some one is by;
but, when I am dying, it is my wish that you should place the pistol in my right hand, and that you
leave me unburied as I lie.” King said that the following morning, about eight o’clock, Burke died.
The student card tells the request more quietly, because this is a Year 5 file. Why might Burke have
asked for that? What can we know, and what can we not?

Teacher Note
CASE 4 · YEAR 5 · TEACHER NOTE


Draft, pending consultation with Yandruwandha Yawarrawarrka and related communities,
and with AIATSIS guidance.


The opening page
The opening page is not constructed, and it must not be labelled “constructed” or “not original” on
the student page. It is an abridged typographic presentation of William John Wills’s last Cooper
Creek field-notebook entry (NLA MS 30/7). Ellipses mark two cuts: the clause “to look for the
blacks,” and a short middle passage about birds and fish, so the page can hold the lines that carry
the case — “no nutriment,” the pulse at forty-eight, “nearly skin and bone,” and the Mr Micawber
sentence — without a graphic account of dying and without mixing in the 30 May cache note. The
closing remarks on fat and sugar were also set aside, so the page ends on the Micawber / nardoo
lines. A full transcription belongs in class only if you have time and a content note ready.

Date of that last entry: this file prints Friday, 28 June 1861, because 28 June 1861 was a Friday.
Some published versions print Friday 26 June (a Wednesday; the NLA catalogue also dates the
notebook 23 April–26 June), or 27 June. Burke and Wills Web flags “Friday, 26 June 1861. [sic: 28
June?].” A provenance note on that site says Burke and King buried the field-book on 28 June. Do
not treat a single heading as settled. Wording also varies. A transcription associated with the NLA
item (and with W. H. Archer’s 1861 copy) has “My pulse are at forty-eight” and “farinacious.” Widely
printed 1863 / later texts have “My pulse is at forty-eight” and “farinaceous.” This file follows the
widely printed wording on the student page and flags the variants here.


What the draft mixed, and what was corrected
The supplied draft presented a “note left at the Dig Tree, 30 May 1861,” and labelled it constructed,
but it mixed the 30 May cache note with later diary lines (“pulse 48,” “skin and bone,” and the
nardoo / “no nutriment” sentence). Those later lines belong to the last notebook entry, not to SLV
MS 13071 SAFE 1. The nutriment wording is genuine, but it is diary, not cache-note. Favenc and
some older printings of the 30 May note also differ in small ways from the two-page SAFE 1
transcription (for example “down on the lower part” / “going fast to pieces”). This file follows the
SAFE 1 transcription as given on burkeandwills.net.au, and puts the note in Super Sleuths, not on
the opening page.


Case number, year level, and curriculum
The draft header was CASE 38 · YEAR 10, with AC9HH10K10 and AC9HH10K11. Those Year 10
codes are rights-and-freedoms content. In this book’s year-level list, Case 38 is already the Wave
Hill walk-off, 1966, and Burke and Wills is already Case 4, Year 5, AC9HS5K03. That v9 Year 5
HASS code concerns the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations Australians
and those who migrated to Australia, in the development of events in an Australian colony. This
written file therefore keeps Case 4, Year 5, AC9HS5K03, and adds the First Nations consultation tag.
It does not overwrite Wave Hill, and it does not silently become Case 38.

pages.text:
Two further flags, for you to raise rather than resolve here. First, the outlined list question was “Why
was no one waiting at the Dig Tree?” The written case uses the draft question, “What was the real
cause of death?” The Dig Tree question is kept as a Super Sleuth. Second, the cause-of-death /
nardoo / Nature 1994 debate may also sit comfortably in Year 9 (Making a nation, 1750–1918). This
file was not moved there.


Dates, names, and other corrections
Return to the depot: evening of 21 April 1861 (King: about half-past seven). Brahe left that morning.
Charles Gray (not Grey in the usual expedition spelling; some newspapers used Grey) died on 17
April 1861, before the depot. Wills’s cache note: 30 May 1861. Burke’s and Wills’s deaths: late June
or very early July 1861; the exact days are not known. King was found on 15 September 1861
(Howitt’s diary; others in the party reached King first that day, then Howitt). Howitt recovered field-
books from the cache later in September (his diary, 28 September).

King’s testimony about Burke’s pistol request is genuine, in the narrative Howitt took down (SLV
MS 13071). The exact wording is in Super Sleuths, not in full on the Year 5 witness card. Earl and
McCleary 1994 is correctly cited as Nature 368, 683–684 (21 April 1994), “Mystery of the poisoned
expedition.” Treat it as a cited hypothesis, not as the verdict.


Portraits, care, and consultation

The Perth Mint Swindle, 1982
This file names living people. It does not say that any living person committed the swindle, or
fabricated evidence. Attribute every claim. The 2004 court quashed the convictions. It did not decide
who obtained the gold. No one has been convicted of the swindle since.
Read the 1989 page through to the last line. Then read what this file can agree on. After that, three
witnesses will be asked the same three questions.

  CASE FILE: PERTH MINT SWINDLE / 1982
  Date of incident      22 June 1982 (gold returned, in part, 1989; convictions quashed 2 July
  2004)
  Location          Perth, Western Australia
  Status    Convictions quashed · Who obtained the gold remains
  undecided
  Key claims still disputed
  – What can the 1982–2004 records actually prove?
  – How far can Lewandowski’s 2002 affidavit be trusted?
  – The court quashed the convictions. Did it decide who obtained the gold?


  WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1982–2008 FILE
  On 22 June 1982, gold left the Perth Mint in exchange for three stolen building-society cheques. The
  quantity is usually given as 49 bars, about 68 kilograms, then valued at about $653,000. Couriers collected
  it. The investigation said it was taken to an office in Subiaco and later towards Jandakot Airport. It then
  disappeared.

  Ray, Peter and Brian Mickelberg were charged and, in 1983, convicted in the District Court of Western
  Australia (Heenan CJDC). Ray was sentenced to 20 years, Peter to 16 years, and Brian to 12 years. Brian’s
  convictions were quashed on appeal in November 1983, and he was released after about nine months. He
  died in a plane crash in 1986.

  In 1989, gold later identified with the missing bullion was sent, anonymously, to Channel 7 in Perth. First,
  a bar was sent to the reporter Alison Fan, with a note. About three months later, gold pellets in containers
  were left at the station. The Mint said the gold matched what had left in 1982. The convictions of Ray and
  Peter still stood.

  In June 2002, former detective Tony Lewandowski swore an affidavit about the investigation. He said that
  he and Don Hancock had fabricated the notes of interview dated 26 July 1982, after 2 September 1982,
  and that evidence they had given about those “confessions” was false. Hancock had died in 2001.
  Lewandowski died in 2004. Hancock was never charged or convicted of fabricating evidence.

  On 2 July 2004 the Court of Criminal Appeal of Western Australia, in Mickelberg v The Queen [2004]
  WASCA 145, allowed the appeals of Ray and Peter, quashed their convictions, and did not order a retrial.

  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The two deliveries in 1989
  Gold later identified with the missing bullion reached Channel 7 in Perth twice in 1989. First, in July,
  a bar was sent to the reporter Alison Fan, with a note. About three months later, gold pellets in
  containers were left at the station after a journalist was tipped off. The Mint said the gold matched
  what had left in 1982.
  The wording of the July note is later reported by ABC News (1 April 2023) as: “The Mickelbergs are
  innocent and rotting in jail.” A contemporaneous 1989 clipping with that exact sentence was not
  located for this file. A second note was reported with the later pellets; its exact wording is not
  securely established here. The opening page uses only the later-reported July sentence, set in type. It
  is not a photograph of the original note.
  Question. What can a returned bar, and a short unsigned sentence, actually prove — and what can
  they not?


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. What the 2004 court decided — and what it did not
  Read Mickelberg v The Queen [2004] WASCA 145 (2 July 2004) on AustLII, at least the orders and
  the majority’s conclusions. The petitioners were Raymond John Mickelberg and Peter Mickelberg.
  Brian was not a petitioner in 2004.
  The majority (Malcolm CJ and Steytler J) allowed the appeals, quashed the convictions, and did not
  order a retrial. They found a substantial miscarriage of justice, and a significant possibility that a
  reasonable jury would have acquitted in the light of the fresh evidence. They held that the remaining
  circumstantial evidence did not make guilt inevitable — including that Peter had not been positively
  identified at the vehicle on 22 June 1982. Murray J dissented. The court did not decide who obtained
  the gold.
  Question. In your own words, separate the court’s orders from the stories people still tell about the
  case.


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. A recanting police witness
  In June 2002, after Don Hancock’s death, Tony Lewandowski swore an affidavit. As later reported

4. The fingerprint — an allegation, not a finding in this file
It has been alleged that a fingerprint used in the case was not honestly obtained. Some later news

On 15 December 2007, Commissioner Karl O’Callaghan issued a public apology on behalf of WA

claims against individuals. A 2021 ex gratia payment has not been found in the sources checked for

gratia payment?

Teacher Note
CASE 41 · YEAR 10 · TEACHER NOTE


This file names living people. It does not say that any living person committed the swindle, or
fabricated evidence. Attribute every claim. The 2004 court quashed the convictions. It did not
decide who obtained the gold. No one has been convicted of the swindle since.


Where this case sits, and why
The user’s draft numbered this Case 39, Year 10, and gave the codes AC9HH10K10 and
AC9HH10K11. In the year-level list, Case 39 is already Zelda D’Aprano and equal pay, 1969. This file
does not overwrite that case. It is placed as Case 41, Year 10, the next free number. Year 10 is the
right band (a late-twentieth-century Australian debate that runs into the 2000s).

AC9HH10K10 and AC9HH10K11 are Year 10 knowledge descriptions about First Nations rights and
freedoms. They are the wrong codes for this file. The honest History knowledge code used here is
AC9HH10K20: different historical interpretations and debates during the second half of the
twentieth century. A related Civics description, AC9HC10K03 (the role of courts and how rights are
protected), may be mentioned to teachers; it is not claimed as a History code on the student pages.


The opening page
The 1989 page is a typographic setting, not a photograph of the original note, and not a facsimile.
That explanation is kept off the student page so the opener can be read as a scene. The only sentence
set as the note is the wording later reported by ABC News, 1 April 2023: “The Mickelbergs are
innocent and rotting in jail.” A contemporaneous 1989 clipping with that exact sentence was not
located for this file. If a teacher has a 1989 source with different wording, the typographic page
should be revised to match the better source, and this note should say so.

There were two deliveries in 1989, not one. In July, a bar was sent to Channel 7 reporter Alison Fan,
with a note. About three months later, pellets in containers were left at the station. A second note
was reported; its exact wording is not securely established here, so it is not quoted as if it were. The
draft’s constructed four-line note (“The Mickelbergs are innocent. / This is from the Mint. / The rest
is still out there. / The police lied.”) was not used, and must not be presented as a real document.
Alison Fan is living: she may be named, but is not given dates, and is not photographed.


Legal care
Do not state or imply, in the book’s voice, that any living person committed the swindle, or that any
living person fabricated evidence, unless a court has found it. Attribute every claim. The 2004 court
(Mickelberg v The Queen [2004] WASCA 145, 2 July 2004) allowed the appeals of Ray and Peter,
quashed their convictions, and ordered no retrial. The majority was Malcolm CJ and Steytler J;
Murray J dissented. The majority found a substantial miscarriage of justice, and a significant
possibility that a reasonable jury would have acquitted in the light of the fresh evidence. It did not
decide who obtained the gold. No one has been convicted of the swindle since. Living people

Silhouettes are used, and are labelled as silhouettes, not likenesses. The court card is a scales
symbol, not a judge’s portrait.

Tony Lewandowski’s 2002 affidavit is a source the 2004 court considered. It is his sworn claim,
reported at the time (including the Sydney Morning Herald, 11 June 2002) and weighed in the
judgment. He admitted that evidence he had given earlier was false. He died in 2004, before the
July judgment. Do not put graphic detail of his death on student pages. Don Hancock (died 2001)
was never charged or convicted of fabricating evidence. Claims about him should remain attributed
(for example, “Lewandowski swore that…”). Hancock’s later public controversies (including Ora
Banda and other unproven matters) are kept off the student pages. They are not proof of what
happened in the 1982–83 Mint investigation.

It has been alleged that a fingerprint was planted or was not honestly obtained. Some later features,
including ABC News on 1 April 2023, have stated that as fact. This file does not. The claim is kept
out of “What is agreed,” and appears in Super Sleuths only as an allegation. The same 2023 feature
places the trial in the Supreme Court; the 2004 judgment records it as a District Court trial before
Heenan CJDC (IND 675 of 1982). Prefer the judgment.

The brief’s reference to a 2021 ex gratia payment and apology was checked and not found. The
documented dates are 15 December 2007 (WA Police apology, Commissioner Karl O’Callaghan, in
the context of a defamation settlement after comments by Assistant Commissioner Mel Hay on 2
July 2004) and 16 January 2008 (State Government ex gratia payment of $500,000 to each of Ray
and Peter, announced by Attorney-General Jim McGinty, in addition to $658,672 already paid
toward legal costs of the 1998 and 2004 appeals). ABC reporting at the time put the combined figure
at more than $1.6 million. The brothers said the offer was “take it or leave it” and too low; they
remained free to pursue civil claims against individuals. The police statement accepted the court’s
decision and acknowledged that Ray and Peter were, and remained, entitled to the presumption of
innocence.

Brian Mickelberg: several reports say his appeal was allowed and his convictions quashed on 4
November 1983, and that he was released after about eight or nine months. ABC News, 1 April 2023,
says his sentence was “cut to eight months.” Those accounts conflict. The student page uses a careful
wording: released after about nine months following an appeal in 1983–84; died in a plane crash in
1986. Do not treat the ABC wording as settled. Sentences at trial are given here as Ray 20 years,
Peter 16 years, Brian 12 years (ABC 2023; the user’s draft; other summaries). One Sydney Morning
Herald piece has referred to a 14-year term for Peter; 16 is the better-attested figure. Ray served a
little over eight years; Peter more than six and a half.

An Australian Financial Review report of the later 1989 pellets described “one of 22 gold bars.” The
usual figure for the 1982 theft is 49 bars, about 68 kilograms, valued at about $653,000 (sometimes
given more exactly as $652,975.24). This file does not adopt “22 bars” on the student pages.

and to sit with an unsolved question without inventing a culprit. The finding options deliberately
include “the records do not prove who obtained the gold” and “we can’t know.” Do not accept a

CASE 42 · YEAR 4 · READ
What can the records still not tell us?
The Unfinished Voyage, 1629
This file is about a shipwreck, and about the records that remain. People died when the ship struck, and
many more were killed later, before help came. This file does not describe those deaths. A note for
teachers is at the end of the case.
Read the page from the night the ship struck. Then read what this file can agree on. After that, three
witnesses will be asked the same three questions.

  CASE FILE: BATAVIA / 1629
  Date of incident      4 June 1629 (wreck found 1963; journal survives in the Dutch archives)
  Location           Houtman Abrolhos, off the coast of what is now Western Australia
  Status     The wreck and the mutiny are not in doubt · The records are still
  unfinished
  Key claims still disputed
  – What can the records still not tell us?
  – Which gaps were never written, and which papers were lost later?
  – Why do later tellings disagree about the numbers?


  WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1629 RECORDS, AND AFTER
  The Batavia was a ship of the Dutch East India Company, the VOC. It left the island of Texel, in the
  Netherlands, in late October 1628, bound for the city then also called Batavia, now Jakarta. Sources do not
  all agree on the exact day it left, or on the exact number of people on board at the start. Many lists say
  about 322 people were on the ship when it struck the reef.

  In the early hours of 4 June 1629 the ship struck a reef in the Houtman Abrolhos, off the coast of what is
  now Western Australia. The journal of the commandeur, Francisco Pelsaert, opens on that Monday
  morning. About 40 people drowned at the wreck. The rest reached low islands nearby. Some later
  retellings give a much higher number for those first deaths. This file keeps the number recorded from the
  Dutch papers: about 40.

  Pelsaert, the skipper Ariaen Jacobsz, and others left in the ship’s longboat to look for water, and then to
  find help. They reached the city of Batavia after a long voyage. Pelsaert came back in a ship called the
  Sardam, in mid-September 1629.

  While they were away, a mutiny was led by the under-merchant Jeronimus Cornelisz. Many people were
  killed before the rescue. A group of soldiers, led by Wiebbe Hayes, found water on a higher island and held
  out. Hayes reached the rescue ship first.

  Pelsaert wrote a long journal. The handwritten journal still survives in the Dutch National Archives. Other
  papers from the ship, including the lists of the crew’s pay, have been lost. The wreck was found in 1963.
  Timbers and objects from the ship are now in the Western Australian Museum.

  No one who was there wrote a full day-by-day record of the weeks of the mutiny as they happened.

The three witness cards are Francisco Pelsaert, Wiebbe Hayes, and the wreck of the Batavia. Further questions —
including why later numbers do not match, the lost pay lists, and two men later left on the mainland — are in

You have a page from the night of the wreck, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The
opening page is one short page about that night. It is not the whole record. Say what you think

What can the records still not tell us?

Why it still matters
The Batavia is often told as a thriller, or as a horror story. The file is still open because some
papers from the ship were lost, because the commandeur was not there for the worst weeks,
and because later tellings do not always agree. Learning to see what a record can prove, and
what it cannot, is the work of this book.

CASE 42 · YEAR 4 · SUPER SLEUTHS
Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. Some
harder parts of this story are kept in the Teacher Note, not here.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/batavia-case/#sleuth


 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
 1. The night the ship struck
 Pelsaert’s journal opens on Monday morning, 4 June 1629, the second day of Whitsuntide, with a
 bright, clear, full moon, on the reef of Frederick Houtman. The Western Australian Museum’s
 account of that night says a white gleam of breaking surf was seen, and that the skipper, Ariaen
 Jacobsz, as head of the watch, took it for moonlight.
 The opening page of this case uses those documented facts, set in type. It is not a photograph of the
 journal, and it is not a whole translation of the entry.
 Question. What can a short opening, written after the shock of the wreck, actually prove — and what
 can it not?


 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
 2. Why the numbers do not match
 Careful museum work often gives about 322 people on board when the ship struck, and about 40 who
 drowned at the wreck. A Western Australian Museum history page also says the ship left Texel on 29
 October 1628 with 341 people. Other pages and books give 27 or 28 October, or “about 330.” The
 National Museum of Australia has said that about 100 people died in the immediate aftermath of the
 collision. That does not match the Dutch papers’ figure of about 40.
 Question. When two museums disagree, what should a case file do instead of picking the more
 dramatic number?


 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
 3. The weeks no commandeur was there to write down
 Pelsaert left in the longboat and came back in mid-September. The worst weeks on the islands
 happened while he was away. His journal of those weeks is not a diary he kept on the spot. It is what
 he later wrote from questions, confessions, and other people’s memories.
 Question. How should we read a record of days the writer did not see?


 STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER

4. Papers that really were lost
Pelsaert’s handwritten journal still survives in the Dutch National Archives (VOC 1098, folios 232–
317). It is not right to say, as a fact, that “pages we know once existed” are missing from that journal,
or that “statements stop mid-sentence,” unless a better source shows that. What has been lost,
according to later museum research, includes the ship’s muster rolls and pay registers, which would
have named the crew.
Question. What is the difference between a page that was never written, and a list that was written
and later lost?


STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. What the museum objects can prove
The wreck was found in 1963. In the 1970s the Western Australian Museum raised part of the stern, a
carved stone portico, and many smaller objects. They prove the ship, and something of what it
carried. They cannot, alone, tell us what was said on the islands.
Question. If you could place one object beside one page of the journal, which two would you choose,
and why?


STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. Other Dutch marks on this coast
The Batavia was not the first Dutch ship on this coast. In 1616 Dirk Hartog left a pewter plate at Cape
Inscription, on what is now Dirk Hartog Island. The plate’s short inscription is complete; it is not an
unfinished fragment. In late 1696 Willem de Vlamingh landed on the island he named ’t Eylandt ’t
Rottenest (Rottnest) and, in 1697, replaced Hartog’s plate with a new one, taking the old plate home.
Each voyage left a different kind of trace: a plate, a journal, a wreck and its objects. That is a better
comparison than a claim that all the Dutch papers have the same “blank stretches.”
Question. What can a plate prove that a journal cannot — and the other way round?


STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. Two men left on the mainland
In mid-November 1629, after the trials on the islands, Pelsaert’s council left two men, Wouter Loos
and Jan Pelgrom de Bye, on the Australian mainland. Their fate is unknown. Later stories about their
lives there, including stories of contact with Aboriginal people of the mid-west coast, have not been
proved. This file does not invent an ending for them.

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
8. A book from 1647, and a journal from 1629
In 1647 a Dutch book, Ongeluckige Voyagie, van’t schip Batavia, was printed from Pelsaert’s journal.
It was popular, and it was reprinted. A printed book is not the same thing as the handwritten journal
in the archives. The 1647 engravings are old and useful, but they are pictures made in Europe, years
later. Some of them are too hard for this year level.
Question. Why might a famous later book still be the wrong proof for a question about the original
journal?
