Teacher Note
CASE 42 · YEAR 4 · TEACHER NOTE


This file is about a shipwreck, and about the records that remain. People died when the ship
struck, and many more were killed later, before help came. This file does not describe those
deaths. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.


Where this case sits, and why
The user’s draft was a Year 4 school-camp investigation, “Batavia Cold Case / The Unfinished
Voyage,” with no case number. In the year-level list, Cases 1–3 are already taken (the First Fleet;
Bennelong and the Governor; Mary Bryant’s escape). This file does not overwrite them. It is placed
as Case 42, Year 4, the next free number. In a teaching sequence it belongs with Year 4, before the
First Fleet, as an earlier European voyage on the Western Australian coast. The sample book keeps
existing numbers, so the case is appended after the written samples.

The book starts at Year 4. Year 3 knowledge descriptions (AC9HS3K01, local community change;
AC9HS3K02, national days, symbols and emblems) do not fit a 1629 VOC voyage. Year 3/4 learners
can still read this file; the honest knowledge code is Year 4. AC9HS4K02 is “the causes of the
establishment of the first British colony in Australia in 1788.” That is not, on its face, a Batavia code.
The official elaborations, though, ask students to examine earlier voyages along the route to
Australia and along the Australian coastline (the examples include Dirk Hartog, Willem Jansz, Abel
Tasman, and James Cook) in order to understand how knowledge of those routes later made a
colony thinkable. The Batavia is a VOC trader, not one of the named explorers in the elaboration.
This file uses AC9HS4K02 by that official path, and says so here. It does not pretend the v9
descriptor is still the old v8 wording about “world navigators, explorers or traders” (ACHASSK084).
The inquiry heart of the case — what sources can and cannot tell us — is also a Year 4 skills matter
(AC9HS4S03, AC9HS4S04). Those skills codes may be mentioned to teachers; they are not claimed
as the History knowledge code on the student pages.


The escape room first
Give students the escape-room story In Case of Emergency first, so they walk the true voyage in
order as background, before they attempt this case. The teacher card How to run it (at the back of
the picture book, and in the app menu) has hooks, grouping, and a debrief. Then open this case file.
The companion app is at https://robmac10.github.io/batavia-escape-room/ ; the QR on the Start
here page uses a small folded story-map emblem, with a you-are-here mark.


The opening page
The opening page is a typographic setting, not a photograph of Pelsaert’s journal, and not a
facsimile. That explanation is kept off the student page so the night can be read as a scene. The date,
the reef of Frederick Houtman, Whitsuntide, and the bright, clear, full moon follow the opening of
Pelsaert’s journal (Nationaal Archief, VOC 1098). The white gleam of surf, and the skipper taking it

for moonlight, follow the Western Australian Museum’s account of that night (Jacobsz as head of
the watch). The English wording is a short rendering for this file, not a long extract copied from a
modern published translation (including Marit van Huystee, 1994, and E. Drok in Henrietta Drake-
Brockman, Voyage to Disaster). If a teacher has a preferred published wording, the typographic page
can be revised to match it, and this note should say so.


Care, and what was not used from the draft
The fuller record of the Batavia includes the murder of many people, including children, sexual
violence, torture used in the later examinations, and executions. None of that is described on the
student pages. A short content note sits at the front of the case. Preview any extra source, including
Mike Dash, Batavia’s Graveyard, and the 1647 engravings, before you share it. Some of those
pictures are too hard for Year 3/4.

The user’s draft was framed as a class file after a school camp, with “museum notes,” “journal
copies,” and “ferry diary pages.” This file is written as a historical case for any classroom, not as a
named camp report, and it does not invent a ferry diary as a 1629 source. The draft said that days in
the records stay short or empty, that numbers do not match, that some statements stop mid-
sentence, and that “pages we know once existed are still missing.” The disagreement about numbers
is real, and is used. The fact that Pelsaert was absent for the mutiny weeks, so those days were not
written as a spot diary, is real, and is used. A general claim that journal pages known to have existed
are missing, or that statements stop mid-sentence, was not established for this file. The manuscript
of the journal survives at folios 232–317. What later research does record as lost includes the ship’s
muster rolls and pay registers (Western Australian Museum, “Databases of the people aboard the
VOC ships”). Those lost lists are the honest example. The draft also compared “unfinished sections”
in the 1616 Hartog plate and in de Vlamingh’s 1696 notes. Hartog’s pewter inscription is short and
complete; de Vlamingh copied it and replaced it in 1697. This file does not invent blank stretches in
those records. Super Sleuths 6 asks a fairer question: what different kinds of trace each Dutch
voyage left.


Facts checked, and flags
Wreck: early hours of 4 June 1629, Morning Reef, Houtman Abrolhos, Wallabi Group. Journal
opening: Monday morning, second day of Whitsuntide, bright clear full moon, reef of Frederick
Houtman. About 40 drowned at the wreck, from the Dutch papers and the Western Australian
Museum’s wreck entry. The National Museum of Australia’s “about 100 people died in the
immediate aftermath” is treated as a conflict, not as the agreed figure. Departure: late October 1628
from Texel. Sources give 27, 28 or 29 October; a 2022 Western Australian Museum history page
gives 29 October and 341 people at departure. About 322 is the figure often given for those on board
at the wreck. The student page uses careful wording and does not silently pick one date. Rescue:
longboat voyage to the city of Batavia; Pelsaert returned on the Sardam in mid-September 1629.
Hayes reached him first and was later promoted to sergeant. Cornelisz led the mutiny; he and others
were tried by the ship’s council. Two men, Wouter Loos and Jan Pelgrom de Bye, were left on the
mainland in mid-November 1629; their fate is unknown. Pelsaert died in September 1630. All of the
1629 people named here are long deceased, so dates may be given. Living archaeologists and

This is not, in the main, a First Nations case, and the envelope is not stamped “Draft, pending
consultation.” The islands and the nearby mainland, though, are part of a coast cared for by
Aboriginal people long before 1629. The two marooned men, and later unproved stories of contact,
are the place where that care is needed. If a class takes Super Sleuths 7 further, it should do so with
the relevant Aboriginal communities of the mid-west coast, and with AIATSIS guidance. This file
does not invent an ending, and it does not name a language group unless a teacher is working with
that community.

No verified contemporary portraits of Pelsaert, Hayes, or Lucretia Jans (also van der Mijlen) were
found for this file. Later paintings sometimes used as “portraits” of them are not their likenesses and
are not used. The witness images are plain silhouettes, or a ship symbol for the wreck.


Curriculum and classroom
Year 4, written so Year 3/4 learners and interested general readers can both stay with it. The useful
work is to sit with an unfinished record without inventing a missing page, and without turning the
case into a horror story. The finding options include “we can’t know.” Lucretia Jans is not a witness
card here: the sources about her include material that is not for this year level. Teachers who
introduce her should preview first, and should not invent a portrait.


Resources
Students can also read the page from the night of the wreck as an interactive book, on a
tablet or phone. The page on screen is the same story as the pages in this book. Use it in
class, or send the link home. The app is built and ready; it should be published only when
you say go. The QR code uses a ship emblem at the centre.

pages.text:
School of Arts, Tenterfield
                                                                      Thursday, 24 October 1889

The great question which they had to consider was, whether the time had not now
arisen for the creation on this Australian continent of an Australian Government, as
distinct from a local Government and an Australian Parliament.

Surely what the Americans had done by war, the Australians could bring about in
peace.

He believed that the time had come, and if two Governments set an example, the
others must soon of necessity follow.

The thing would have to be done, and to put it off would only tend to make the
difficulties which stood in the way greater.

                                             Queen’s Hall, Parliament House, Melbourne

WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1889–1902 RECORDS, AND AFTER
  Sir Henry Parkes, five times Premier of New South Wales, spoke at a banquet in the School of Arts at
  Tenterfield on 24 October 1889. He called for an Australian government and an Australian parliament,
  and for a convention to draw up a constitution. The next morning, The Sydney Morning Herald printed a
  long report of the speech, mostly in reported speech — “he said,” “they had to consider” — not as a word-
  for-word script in the first person.

  On 6 February 1890, at a banquet in Melbourne for the Australasian Federation Conference, Parkes
  responded to the toast “A United Australasia.” The line most often remembered from that night is: “The
  crimson thread of kinship runs through us all.” In the same speech he spoke of a shared British origin.
  That “us” did not include everyone who lived on this continent.

  Parkes died in Sydney on 27 April 1896. He did not see 1 January 1901, when the Commonwealth of
  Australia came into being at a ceremony in Centennial Park, Sydney. Edmund Barton became the first
  Prime Minister.

  The Constitution had been agreed to in referendums, colony by colony, in 1898, 1899 and 1900, and then
  passed by the British Parliament. Who could vote in those referendums was not the same in every colony.
  In most colonies the voters were adult men. Women could already vote in South Australia, and, from 1899,
  in Western Australia, and they could take part in the later referendums there. Aboriginal people were not
  treated the same way in every colony. In Western Australia, and in Queensland, most Aboriginal people
  were kept off the roll. The picture is more complicated in some other colonies, and this file does not
  pretend it was simple.

  The Constitution, as it stood in 1901, said two things that matter for this case. Section 127 said that, in
  reckoning the numbers of the people, “aboriginal natives shall not be counted.” Section 51(xxvi), the “race
  power,” gave the Commonwealth Parliament power to make special laws for “the people of any race, other
  than the aboriginal race in any State.” Both provisions were later changed, in 1967. This file does not treat
  1967 as the end of the story.

  On 12 June 1902 the Commonwealth Franchise Act became law. It gave the federal vote to men and
  women who were twenty-one or over, British subjects, resident, and on the roll — and then shut many
  people out. It said: “No aboriginal native of Australia Asia Africa or the Islands of the Pacific except New
  Zealand shall be entitled to have his name placed on an Electoral Roll unless so entitled under section
  forty-one of the Constitution.” Section 41, and how it was later read, is still argued over. In 1901 the new
  Parliament also passed the Immigration Restriction Act, which used a dictation test to keep many people
  out.

  New Zealand did not join the Commonwealth. Parkes had spoken of “Australasia” at the 1890 banquet; the
  nation that began in 1901 was the six Australian colonies.


Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.

The three witness cards are Edmund Barton, Rose Scott, and Mei Quong Tart. Further questions — including who
could vote in the referendums, section 127, the 1902 Franchise Act, and what “us all” included — are in Super

There is no answer at the back. The records show that some people had a vote, and that some
people were written out of the count and out of the roll. They do not capture every voice that
was never asked. Write only what these records can support. Do not invent what they do not

Why it still matters
The speeches still tell us who was meant by “us all.” The Constitution, and the Franchise Act
that followed, still show who was counted, who could vote, and who was left out. Section 127,
and the wording of the race power, were later changed, in 1967. The franchise later widened.
Those changes matter, and they do not close the file. The question of who gets a say in the
nation is not only a question about 1901.

CASE 13 · YEAR 6 · SUPER SLEUTHS
Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. This
file is a draft, pending consultation, wherever it touches First Nations histories.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/federation-case/#sleuth


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  1. The Herald’s Parkes, not a rewritten “I”
  The typographic page follows The Sydney Morning Herald of 25 October 1889, p. 8. The speech was
  given on 24 October. The Herald mostly used reported speech: “the great question which they had to
  consider was…” Later retellings, including some museum pages, turn this into first person (“we have
  to consider”). This file does not make that change.
  Question. Why might a later writer change “they” to “we,” and what is lost when that happens?


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  2. “The crimson thread of kinship”
  This line is from the Melbourne banquet of 6 February 1890, not from Tenterfield. In the same
  speech Parkes spoke of a shared British origin. “Us all” was a claim about kinship. It was not a claim
  that every person on this continent was included. Aboriginal people, and many Chinese-Australians,
  were outside that “thread” as Parkes drew it.
  Question. If a speaker says “us all,” how can you tell who is meant?


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  3. He never saw it happen
  Tenterfield, 24 October 1889. Melbourne banquet, 6 February 1890. Parkes died on 27 April 1896.
  The Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901. The handover line in this file is not a quotation from
  Parkes. It is this file’s plain statement of those dates.
  Question. Why might it matter that the man later called the “Father of Federation” — a later title, not
  a name he gave himself on the typographic page — never saw the ceremony?


  STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
  4. Who could vote in the referendums
  The Constitution was put to voters in 1898, 1899 and 1900. The rules were not the same in every
  colony. Women could vote in South Australia, and, from 1899, in Western Australia. In most other

colonies the voters were adult men. Aboriginal people were widely excluded in Queensland and
Western Australia. In some other colonies the picture is more complicated, and summaries
sometimes flatten it. New South Wales’s 1898 result is often told as a majority that still failed a
special threshold; later votes went the other way. Western Australia voted in 1900. New Zealand did
not join.
Question. Why is “the people voted for Federation” too simple a sentence?


STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Section 127, and the race power
Section 127 of the Constitution, as it stood in 1901, said that in reckoning the numbers of the people,
“aboriginal natives shall not be counted.” Section 51(xxvi) gave the Commonwealth power to make
special laws for “the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State.” Both were
changed in 1967. This file does not treat those later changes as if they cancelled the 1901 record, or as
if they ended every question about who counts.
Question. What is the difference between not being counted, and not being allowed to vote?


STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. The 1902 Franchise Act, and section 41
The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902, assented to on 12 June, gave the federal vote to men and
women who met its tests — and then said: “No aboriginal native of Australia Asia Africa or the
Islands of the Pacific except New Zealand shall be entitled to have his name placed on an Electoral
Roll unless so entitled under section forty-one of the Constitution.” Section 41 is a difficult clause.
Later governments and courts often read it narrowly. This file flags that dispute rather than settling
it.
Question. Why might a law that is remembered for giving women the federal vote also be a record of
who was shut out?


STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. Quong Tart’s letter, and the dictation test
The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 used a dictation test to keep many people out. On 8 January
1903 Quong Tart wrote to Barton about how that law was affecting Chinese people. The National
Archives of Australia describes the letter; this file has not printed a word-for-word extract, because it
has not checked a full transcription against the original in this build. In 1894, Sir Henry Parkes had
written a letter of introduction for Quong Tart, praising his “energy and integrity.” Parkes’s “crimson
thread” and Parkes’s respect for one Chinese-Australian merchant can both be in the record.

CASE 13 · YEAR 6 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher Note
Draft, pending consultation. This case asks who was left out of the new nation, including
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Teach it with care. Follow AIATSIS guidance, and
do not treat this file as a finished account of First Nations experience. The user’s name is kept
off the student pages and off the app.


What is quoted, and what is framing
The typographic page is not a facsimile of a newspaper, and it is not a diary. It is a typographic
setting of verified wording. The Tenterfield lines are taken from The Sydney Morning Herald,
25 October 1889, p. 8, which reported the banquet speech of 24 October. The Herald used
reported speech. This file keeps “they had to consider,” “had done,” “could bring about,” and
“He believed that the time had come.” It does not rewrite those lines as “I” or “we.” Some later
museum and classroom pages do make that change. The Teacher Note flags them, rather than
following them.
The last line on the typographic page, “The crimson thread of kinship runs through us all,” is
from Parkes’s response to the toast “A United Australasia” at the Federation Conference
banquet in Queen’s Hall, Parliament House, Melbourne, on 6 February 1890. It is not from
Tenterfield. It is one of the most widely attested sentences in the Federation story. Teachers
should still check a contemporary report (The Argus or The Age, 7 February 1890, or a careful
later printing) beside this page.
“He never saw it happen” is this file’s handover. It is not a quotation from Parkes. The dates
under it are not in dispute: he died on 27 April 1896; the Commonwealth began on 1 January
1901. The file does not invent a Centennial Park scene in his voice, or a child’s invented diary of
that morning, on the student pages.


Care, and conflicts this file will not settle
Who could vote in each referendum is not a single rule. Women voted in South Australia, and in
Western Australia from 1899. Aboriginal voting was restricted or denied in Queensland and
Western Australia; elsewhere the picture is more complicated, and secondary summaries
sometimes flatten it. Section 41 of the Constitution, and how it was later applied to people
already on a state roll, is still argued over. The 1902 Act’s exclusion is quoted from the Act itself
(assented 12 June 1902). “Father of Federation” is a later title. Barton’s “nation for a continent”
line is kept at Ashfield, 1897, not moved to 1 January 1901. This file summarises Quong Tart’s 8
January 1903 letter from the National Archives’ description; it does not print a word-for-word
extract, because a full checked transcription of that letter was not in hand for this build.
Parkes’s 1 March 1894 letter of introduction for Quong Tart is in the State Library of New South
Wales papers.
Rose Scott’s card does not invent a quotation. A later parliamentary-library account has been
cited elsewhere for words of hers about race, colour, and the 1902 franchise. Those words were
